content: Individuals who have experienced failure in one or more full-thickness penetrating keratoplasties may be candidates for repeat corneal transplantation. This can involve the use of either a donor cornea or an artificial cornea, also referred to as a keratoprosthesis. Both procedures require the removal of the diseased or previously failed cornea and its replacement with either a donor cornea or a prosthetic device. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of artificial corneas compared to donor corneas in patients who have undergone one or more failed donor corneal transplants. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. The last search was performed on November 4, 2019. Two independent reviewers assessed the search results to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or controlled clinical trials that met the inclusion criteria. Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed during the review process. However, no data synthesis was performed, as no eligible trials were identified. Instead, findings from relevant comparative case series were summarized for discussion purposes. The review did not identify any RCTs or controlled clinical trials that directly compared artificial corneas with donor corneas for repeat corneal transplantation. Consequently, the optimal approach for managing patients who have failed a conventional corneal transplant remains unclear. Current practices vary significantly between centers. In some institutions, artificial corneal devices are recommended after a single graft failure, while in others, they are only considered after multiple graft failures or not recommended at all. To date, there is a lack of controlled trials comparing the visual outcomes and complications associated with artificial corneal devices, particularly the Boston type 1 keratoprosthesis (the most commonly implanted artificial cornea), to those of repeat donor corneal transplantation. Such a trial is urgently needed to provide evidence-based guidance for surgeons and their patients. This would be especially beneficial for the growing number of individuals with visual impairment due to corneal opacification, many of whom are in the productive stages of their lives.
